INSTRUCTIONS TO RUN THIS R MARKDOWN FILE

1) Install required libraries — see install_packages.R at the repo root.
2) Download the full "Credit Score Classification" dataset from Kaggle
   (Rohan Paris, 2022, CC BY 4.0):
   https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/parisrohan/credit-score-classification
   Place train.csv under data/raw/ at the REPO ROOT (not committed to this repo —
   see data/sample/credit_risk_sample_200.csv for a 200-row preview of the
   cleaned/encoded schema instead).
3) Note: rmarkdown::render() knits with this file's own folder (r_analysis/) as
   the working directory by default, not the repo root — that's why the paths
   below start with "../". If you move this file, update the paths to match.
4) Run the entire script sequentially. All intermediate CSV/PNG outputs are
   written to the working directory (r_analysis/), matching the copies already
   committed under results/.

```{r}
#Importing the CSV file and eyeballing the data
# Full 100,000-row raw dataset (Kaggle, CC BY 4.0) — download separately, see
# instructions above. A 200-row cleaned/encoded sample is committed at
# data/sample/credit_risk_sample_200.csv for reference.

mydf <- read.csv("../data/raw/train.csv", na.strings = c("NA",""))
summary(mydf)
```

```{r}
# Data Cleaning

# Converting categorical variables to factors
categorical_cols <- c('Month', 'Name', 'Occupation', 'Type_of_Loan', 'Credit_Mix', 
                      'Payment_of_Min_Amount', 'Payment_Behaviour', 'Credit_Score')

mydf <- mydf %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(categorical_cols), as.factor))

# Handle special characters and invalid values in numeric columns
# First, identify numeric columns
numeric_cols <- mydf %>%
  select(-all_of(categorical_cols), -ID, -Customer_ID, -SSN, -Credit_History_Age) %>%
  names()

#Replace any _ with empty strings
mydf <- data.frame(lapply(mydf, function(x) gsub("_", "", x)))
#fill the empty strings with NAs
mydf <- data.frame(lapply(mydf, function(x) ifelse(x == "", NA, x)))

# Clean credit history age (convert to months)
mydf <- mydf %>%
  mutate(
    Credit_History_Age = str_replace_all(Credit_History_Age, "NA", ""),
    Credit_History_Age = ifelse(Credit_History_Age == "", NA, Credit_History_Age),
    Credit_History_Months = case_when(
      grepl("Years and", Credit_History_Age) ~ 
        as.numeric(str_extract(Credit_History_Age, "\\d+(?= Years)")) * 12 + 
        as.numeric(str_extract(Credit_History_Age, "\\d+(?= Months)")),
      grepl("Years", Credit_History_Age) ~ 
        as.numeric(str_extract(Credit_History_Age, "\\d+")) * 12,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

# Ensuring numerical variables are numeric
mydf <- mydf %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(numeric_cols), as.numeric))
mydf <-  mydf %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(categorical_cols), as.factor))

#Cleaning the special characters and replacing it with NA values
mydf <- mydf %>%
  mutate(Payment_Behaviour = ifelse(as.character(Payment_Behaviour) == "!@9#%8", NA, as.character(Payment_Behaviour)),
         Payment_Behaviour = factor(Payment_Behaviour))

summary(mydf)
```

Creation of the target variable
```{r}
# Creating a new column for assessing Low or High Risk which supports our Research Question and will be our Target Variable
mydf$Risk <- ifelse(mydf$Credit_Score == "Poor", "High", "Low")
mydf$Risk <- as.factor(mydf$Risk)
```

Removing unnecessary features
```{r}
# Columns to remove ID, Customer ID, Name, SSN, Credit History Age(after converting to months) as they are redundant identifiers
mydf <- mydf %>% select(-ID, -Customer_ID, -Name, -SSN, -Credit_History_Age, -Type_of_Loan, -Credit_Score)
```

```{r}
# Substituting all numerical NA Values with median/mode (N Age Median, C Occupation Mode, N Monthly_Inhand_Salary, C Type_of_Loan,
# N Num_of_Delayed_Payment, N Changed_Credit_Limit, N Num_Credit_Inquiries, C Credit_Mix, N Amount_invested_monthly,
# C Payment_Behaviour, N Monthly_Balance, N Credit_History_Months)

numeric_cols <- sapply(mydf, is.numeric)
categorical_cols <- sapply(mydf, is.factor)

mydf <- mydf %>%
  mutate(
    Age = ifelse(Age < 0 | Age > 120, NA, Age),
    Num_Bank_Accounts = ifelse(Num_Bank_Accounts < 0, NA, Num_Bank_Accounts),
    Num_of_Loan = ifelse(Num_of_Loan < 0, NA, Num_of_Loan),
    Delay_from_due_date = ifelse(Delay_from_due_date < 0, NA, Delay_from_due_date),
    Num_of_Delayed_Payment = ifelse(Num_of_Delayed_Payment < 0, NA, Num_of_Delayed_Payment),
    Changed_Credit_Limit = ifelse(Changed_Credit_Limit < 0, NA, Changed_Credit_Limit)
  )

#Checking the percentage of NA values for the entire dataset
mydf_NA_count <- apply(is.na(mydf), 2, sum)
mydf_NA_perc <- mydf_NA_count / dim(mydf)[1] * 100
mydf_NA_perc
```

```{r}
# Median imputation for numeric features

for (col_name in names(mydf)[numeric_cols]) {
  # Replace NA values with the median of the column
  mydf[[col_name]][is.na(mydf[[col_name]])] <- median(mydf[[col_name]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

#Checking the percentage of NA values for the entire dataset after removing NA values for the numerical variables
mydf_NA_count <- apply(is.na(mydf), 2, sum)
mydf_NA_perc <- mydf_NA_count / dim(mydf)[1] * 100
mydf_NA_perc
```

```{r}
# Mode imputation for categorical features
Mode <- function(x) { ux <- unique(x[!is.na(x)]); ux[which.max(tabulate(match(x, ux)))] }
for(col in names(mydf)[categorical_cols]) {
  mode_val <- Mode(mydf[[col]])
  mydf[[col]][is.na(mydf[[col]])] <- mode_val
}

#Checking the percentage of NA values for the entire dataset after removing NA values for the categorical variables
mydf_NA_count <- apply(is.na(mydf), 2, sum)
mydf_NA_perc <- mydf_NA_count / dim(mydf)[1] * 100
mydf_NA_perc
```

```{r}
# Outlier Detection

# Defining a function to replace outliers with median
replace_outliers_with_median <- function(data, column_name) {
  outliers <- boxplot(data[[column_name]], plot = FALSE)$out
  data[[column_name]] <- ifelse(data[[column_name]] %in% outliers, NA, data[[column_name]])
  data[[column_name]][is.na(data[[column_name]])] <- median(data[[column_name]], na.rm = TRUE)
  print(summary(data[[column_name]]))
  return(data)
}

# Apply the function to all relevant numerical columns
columns_to_process <- c(
  "Num_Bank_Accounts", "Num_Credit_Card", "Interest_Rate", "Num_of_Loan",
  "Num_of_Delayed_Payment", "Num_Credit_Inquiries", "Total_EMI_per_month",
  "Amount_invested_monthly", "Annual_Income"
)

for (col in columns_to_process) {
  mydf <- replace_outliers_with_median(mydf, col)
}

summary(mydf)
```

-----------------------
ENCODING

Checking if the categorical variables are significant enough to stay or we would remove them. One-Hot encoding is preferred as the models will treat the
numerically labeled values as ordinal variables.
```{r}
#Will have One-Hot encoding
table(mydf$Payment_of_Min_Amount,mydf$Risk)
chisq.test(mydf$Payment_of_Min_Amount,mydf$Risk)
```

```{r}
#Will have One-Hot encoding
table(mydf$Payment_Behaviour,mydf$Risk)
chisq.test(mydf$Payment_Behaviour,mydf$Risk)
```

```{r}
#Will have One-Hot encoding
table(mydf$Occupation,mydf$Risk)
chisq.test(mydf$Occupation,mydf$Risk)
```

```{r}
#Will have One-Hot encoding
table(mydf$Credit_Mix,mydf$Risk)
chisq.test(mydf$Credit_Mix,mydf$Risk)
```

```{r}

#Encoding values for Risk, Occupation, Credit_mix, Payment_Behaviour, Payment_of_Min_Amount
mydf$Risk <- factor(mydf$Risk, levels = c("Low", "High"))
# create a numeric version: Low → 0, High → 1
mydf$Risk <- as.integer(mydf$Risk) - 1
mydf$Risk <- as.factor(mydf$Risk)

# Ensure the selected columns are factors
mydf$Occupation <- as.factor(mydf$Occupation)
mydf$Credit_Mix <- as.factor(mydf$Credit_Mix)
mydf$Payment_Behaviour <- as.factor(mydf$Payment_Behaviour)
mydf$Payment_of_Min_Amount <- as.factor(mydf$Payment_of_Min_Amount)

# Create one-hot encoded variables
occupation_dummies <- model.matrix(~ Occupation - 1, data = mydf)
creditmix_dummies <- model.matrix(~ Credit_Mix - 1, data = mydf)
paymentbehaviour_dummies <- model.matrix(~ Payment_Behaviour - 1, data = mydf)
paymentminamount_dummies <- model.matrix(~ Payment_of_Min_Amount - 1, data = mydf)

# Combine the dummy variables with the original dataframe (excluding the original categorical columns)
mydf <- cbind(
  mydf[ , !(names(mydf) %in% c("Occupation", "Credit_Mix", "Payment_Behaviour", "Payment_of_Min_Amount"))],
  occupation_dummies,
  creditmix_dummies,
  paymentbehaviour_dummies,
  paymentminamount_dummies
)


str(mydf)
```
-----------------------
Sampling

Based on the EDA observation, there was a noticeable class imbalance. To mitigate this we have used stratified sampling to divide the Risk class in equal proportions.
The below code is divided into 5000 rows each Risk type to reduce modelling training time and computational cost.
```{r}
mydf$ID <- 1:nrow(mydf)
set.seed(123)
#----------------------
#This commented code was used to extract the csv file for HPCI implementation where 28998 rows were extracted for 0 and 1 risk types
#stratified_sample <- strata(mydf, stratanames = "Risk", size = rep(28998, length(unique(mydf$Risk))), method = "srswor")
#mydf_ready <- mydf[stratified_sample$ID_unit, ]
#mydf_ready <- mydf_ready %>% select(-ID)
#write.csv(mydf_ready,"HPCI_Cleaned_Data.csv")
#----------------------
stratified_sample <- strata(mydf, stratanames = "Risk", size = rep(5000, length(unique(mydf$Risk))), method = "srswor")
mydf_ready <- mydf[stratified_sample$ID_unit, ]
mydf_ready <- mydf_ready %>% select(-ID)

#Checking the proportions
prop.table(table(mydf_ready$Risk))
```

PCA for Dimensionality Reduction

```{r}
pca_result <- prcomp(mydf_ready %>% select_if(is.numeric) , center=T ,scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca_result)
```
PCA Loadings
```{r}
plot(pca_result)
```

Proportion of Explained Variance that would help identifying the ideal number of PCs which explains the most of the variance in our dataset.
```{r}
pca_result_var <- pca_result$sdev^2
pca_result_PEV <- pca_result_var / sum(pca_result_var)

# plot the cumulative value of PEV for increasing number of additional PCs
#   note: add an 80% threshold line to inform the feature extraction
#     according to the plot the first 3 PCs should be selected
opar <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
plot(
  cumsum(pca_result_PEV),
  ylim = c(0,1),
  xlab = 'PC',
  ylab = 'Cumulative PEV',
  #pch = 20,
  col = 'orange'
)
abline(h = 0.8, col = 'red', lty = 'dashed')
par(opar)
```

-------------
Clustering

We are going with K-means as the dataset has a large number of features.

```{r}
# Elbow Method to determine optimal number of clusters
fviz_nbclust(pca_result$x, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 10) +
  labs(title = "Elbow Method for Optimal K") +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r}
#We are going for values 2 and 3 for the K as the elbow method shows Sharp drop from k=1 → k=2. Big reduction in within-cluster sum of squares.
#Better smoother decline from k=2 → k=3. Still some reduction, but less sharp.
pca_dis <- pca_result$x
distance <- dist(pca_dis, method='euclidean')
k_means_result1 <- kmeans(pca_dis, 3)
k_means_result_id1 <- k_means_result1$cluster
k_means_sil1 <- cluster::silhouette(k_means_result_id1, distance)
plot(k_means_sil1, col = "red", border = NA, main = "Silhouette Plot", cex.names = 0.6)
```

Going. with 2 clusters
```{r}
k_means_result2 <- kmeans(pca_dis, 2)
k_means_result_id2 <- k_means_result2$cluster
k_means_sil2 <- cluster::silhouette(k_means_result_id2, distance)
plot(k_means_sil2, col = "red", border = NA, main = "Silhouette Plot", cex.names = 0.6)
```
Decided to go with 2 as the Average Silhoutte Width is better.
-----------------------
Train/Test Split

Going with the Hold-out method of splitting the data into 70-30 proportions having an equal distribution of Risk factors in each set.
```{r}
# Make sure Risk is a factor
mydf_ready$Risk <- factor(mydf_ready$Risk)

# Calculate proportional class counts for training set (70%)
train_props <- prop.table(table(mydf_ready$Risk)) * floor(0.7 * nrow(mydf_ready))
train_props <- round(train_props)
names(train_props) <- levels(mydf_ready$Risk)  # Ensure names match factor levels

# Stratified sampling: get training indices
set.seed(42)  # for reproducibility
train_indices <- unlist(
  lapply(levels(mydf_ready$Risk), function(risk_level) {
    rows_in_class <- which(mydf_ready$Risk == risk_level)
    sample(rows_in_class, train_props[[risk_level]])
  })
)

# Create train/test sets
train_set <- mydf_ready[train_indices, ]
test_set <- mydf_ready[-train_indices, ]

# Check class balance
cat("Training set distribution:\n")
print(table(train_set$Risk))
cat("Test set distribution:\n")
print(table(test_set$Risk))

```

```{r}
# Since the pre-processing, sampling and cleaning is done. Verifying the entire dataset before proceeding with modelling.
str(train_set)
str(test_set)
```

# Random Forest Model Section

```{r}
# setting levels for Risk
levels(train_set$Risk) <- c("High", "Low")
levels(test_set$Risk) <- c("High", "Low")
```


Part 1: Benchmark Supporting Model (Logistic Regression)
A logistic regression model was built on the cleaned dataset to establish a baseline for performance evaluation. As a straightforward, interpretable linear classifier, it established a preliminary benchmark for accuracy and AUC. Evaluation criteria were documented using a confusion matrix and ROC curve to assess enhancements from more sophisticated models.

1. Logistic Regression: logit_model

```{r}
# Train Logistic Regression
set.seed(42)
logit_model <- glm(Risk ~ ., data = train_set, family = "binomial")

```

```{r}
# Predict and evaluate
logit_probs <- predict(logit_model, test_set, type = "response")
logit_pred <- ifelse(logit_probs > 0.5, "Low", "High")  # Assuming 1 = "Low" (positive)
logit_pred <- factor(logit_pred, levels = c("High", "Low"))  # Match factor levels

# Confusion Matrix
confusionMatrix(logit_pred, test_set$Risk)

# AUC
roc_logit <- roc(test_set$Risk, logit_probs)
cat("Logistic Regression AUC:", auc(roc_logit), "\n")

```


Part 2: Multiple Random Forest Model Experiments (RF1–RF6) (testing & tuning)

Six Random Forest models were developed to explore the effects of different hyperparameter configurations:

RF1 (Default): Basic model using default settings.

RF2 (Tuned): Cross-validated model using caret with a tuned mtry parameter.

RF3 (Deep): Larger trees (low nodesize, more depth).

RF4 (Shallow): Smaller trees (higher nodesize, limited depth).

RF5 (V2): Manual setup using mtry = sqrt(p) and ntree = 1000.

RF6 (V3): Custom forest using mtry = p/3 and maxnodes = 30.

All models were evaluated using accuracy, confusion matrix, and AUC on the same test set. These comparisons helped identify the setup that optimally balanced complexity, performance, and generality.

1: RF1: Basic Random Forest (Default Random Forest)

```{r}
# RF1: Basic Random Forest
set.seed(42)
rf_default <- randomForest(Risk ~ ., data = train_set, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
```

2: RF2: Tuned Random Forest (Tuned Random Forest using caret)

```{r}
# RF2: Tuned Random Forest
set.seed(42)

# Define 5-fold cross-validation
control <- trainControl(method="cv", number=5, classProbs=TRUE, summaryFunction=twoClassSummary)

# Grid for mtry values
rf_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12))

# Train
rf_tuned <- train(
  Risk ~ ., 
  data = train_set, 
  method = "rf", 
  metric = "ROC", 
  trControl = control, 
  tuneGrid = rf_grid, 
  ntree = 500
)

# best mtry value selected
cat("Best mtry value selected by cross-validation:\n")
print(rf_tuned$bestTune)

# ROC performance for each mtry value
cat("\nFull cross-validation results:\n")
print(rf_tuned$results)
```

3: RF3: Deeper Trees (Deeper Random Forest - bigger trees)

```{r}
# RF3: Deeper Trees
set.seed(42)
rf_deep <- randomForest(
  Risk ~ ., 
  data = train_set, 
  ntree = 1000, 
  mtry = 8,          # Adjusting value based on best mtry from RF2
  nodesize = 2, 
  importance = TRUE
)
```

4: RF4: Shallow Trees (Shallow Random Forest - smaller trees)

```{r}
# RF4: Shallow Trees
set.seed(42)
rf_shallow <- randomForest(
  Risk ~ ., 
  data = train_set, 
  ntree = 300, 
  mtry = 4, 
  nodesize = 10, 
  importance = TRUE
)
```

5: RF5: Build RF_V2 (1000 trees, mtry = sqrt(p))

```{r}
# RF5: RF_V2 (1000 trees, mtry = sqrt(p))
set.seed(42)
rf_v2 <- randomForest(Risk ~ ., data = train_set, ntree = 1000, mtry = floor(sqrt(ncol(train_set) - 1)))
```

6: RF6: Build RF_V3 (1000 trees, mtry = p/3, maxnodes = 30)

```{r}
# RF6: RF_V3 (1000 trees, mtry = p/3, maxnodes = 30)
set.seed(42)
rf_v3 <- randomForest(Risk ~ ., data = train_set, ntree = 1000, mtry = floor((ncol(train_set) - 1) / 3), maxnodes = 30)
```

Predict on Test Set for Each Model

```{r}
# Predictions
pred_default  <- predict(rf_default, test_set)
pred_tuned    <- predict(rf_tuned, test_set)
pred_deep     <- predict(rf_deep, test_set)
pred_shallow  <- predict(rf_shallow, test_set)
pred_v2       <- predict(rf_v2, test_set)
pred_v3       <- predict(rf_v3, test_set)

```

Evaluate Performance: Accuracy, Confusion Matrix

```{r}
# Confusion Matrices
confusionMatrix(pred_default, reference = test_set$Risk)
confusionMatrix(pred_tuned, reference = test_set$Risk)
confusionMatrix(pred_deep, reference = test_set$Risk)
confusionMatrix(pred_shallow, reference = test_set$Risk)
confusionMatrix(pred_v2, reference = test_set$Risk)
confusionMatrix(pred_v3, reference = test_set$Risk)

```

ROC AUC Calculations

```{r}
# Probabilities for AUC
probs_default  <- predict(rf_default, test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]
probs_tuned    <- predict(rf_tuned, test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]
probs_deep     <- predict(rf_deep, test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]
probs_shallow  <- predict(rf_shallow, test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]
probs_v2       <- predict(rf_v2, test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]
probs_v3       <- predict(rf_v3, test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]

# ROC Curves
roc_default  <- roc(test_set$Risk, probs_default)
roc_tuned    <- roc(test_set$Risk, probs_tuned)
roc_deep     <- roc(test_set$Risk, probs_deep)
roc_shallow  <- roc(test_set$Risk, probs_shallow)
roc_v2       <- roc(test_set$Risk, probs_v2)
roc_v3       <- roc(test_set$Risk, probs_v3)

# Print AUCs
cat("RF1 (Default) AUC:", auc(roc_default), "\n")
cat("RF2 (Tuned) AUC:", auc(roc_tuned), "\n")
cat("RF3 (Deep) AUC:", auc(roc_deep), "\n")
cat("RF4 (Shallow) AUC:", auc(roc_shallow), "\n")
cat("RF5 (V2) AUC:", auc(roc_v2), "\n")
cat("RF6 (V3) AUC:", auc(roc_v3), "\n")

```

Part 3: Final Tuned Random Forest Model
A final model was chosen and trained utilising insights from RF2 and other variants.Caret with 5-fold cross-validation with ntree set to 1000 was used for this model. The finalised model underwent comprehensive evaluation.

Metrics: Accuracy, Area Under the Curve (AUC), precision, recall, F1 score.

Visuals: ROC curves, feature importance (both Gini and Accuracy), and ROC overlays for comparative model analysis.

Results: All outputs are saved in CSV and PNG formats for documentation and reproducibility.

Final Random Forest Model

```{r}

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)

# 5-fold cross-validation setup
control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 5,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary
)

# Grid of mtry values to test
rf_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12))

# Train the tuned Random Forest model
rf_final <- train(
  Risk ~ ., 
  data = train_set, 
  method = "rf", 
  metric = "ROC", 
  trControl = control, 
  tuneGrid = rf_grid, 
  ntree = 1000
)

# Best mtry value selected
cat("Best mtry value selected by cross-validation:\n")
print(rf_final$bestTune)

# ROC performance for each mtry value
cat("\nFull cross-validation results:\n")
print(rf_final$results)

# Plot ROC vs mtry (optional)
ggplot(rf_final$results, aes(x = mtry, y = ROC)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "ROC vs mtry",
       x = "mtry (Number of Variables Tried at Each Split)",
       y = "ROC Score") +
  theme_minimal()

write.csv(rf_final$results, "rf_cv_results.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

```{r}
# Predict
pred_final   <- predict(rf_final, test_set)
```

```{r}
# Accuracy and confusion matrices
levels(test_set$Risk)

cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_final, reference = test_set$Risk)

# Extract overall and class metrics
overall_metrics <- as.data.frame(t(cm$overall))
colnames(overall_metrics) <- paste0("Overall_", colnames(overall_metrics))

class_metrics <- as.data.frame(t(cm$byClass))
colnames(class_metrics) <- paste0("Class_", colnames(class_metrics))

# Combine all
all_metrics <- cbind(overall_metrics, class_metrics)

# Save all to CSV
write.csv(all_metrics, "rf_full_evaluation_metrics.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# Probabilities for AUC
probs_final  <- predict(rf_final, test_set, type = "prob")[, 2]

# ROC Curve and AUC
roc_final  <- roc(test_set$Risk, probs_final)
auc_val <- auc(roc_final)
cat("RF (Final) AUC:", round(auc_val, 4), "\n")

# Predict class labels
pred_final <- predict(rf_final, test_set)

# Confusion matrix
cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_final, reference = test_set$Risk)

# Extract metrics
precision <- cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]
recall    <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]
f1_score  <- 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)

# Print to console
cat("Precision:", round(precision, 4), "\n")
cat("Recall:", round(recall, 4), "\n")
cat("F1 Score:", round(f1_score, 4), "\n")

# Save all metrics into a data frame
metrics_df <- data.frame(
  AUC = round(auc_val, 4),
  Precision = round(precision, 4),
  Recall = round(recall, 4),
  F1_Score = round(f1_score, 4)
)

# Write to CSV
write.csv(metrics_df, "rf_final_metrics.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

-----------------------
Statistical Significance Check (DeLong's Test) — added for this repo

The written report (Section 6.2) cites DeLong's test for several AUC comparisons, including
a cross-platform check (R Random Forest vs. Spark Random Forest: z = 3.67, p < 0.001). That
specific comparison spans two different held-out samples (3,000 rows in R vs. ~17,400 in
Spark) and its underlying script was not preserved among the submitted materials, so it is
reported in this repo's README as a documented finding rather than re-executed here.

What *is* fully reproducible end-to-end in this file is a paired DeLong test on the two
models that share the identical `test_set`: the Final Tuned Random Forest against the
Logistic Regression baseline.

```{r}
# DeLong's test: Final Random Forest vs. Logistic Regression baseline
# (paired — both evaluated on the same held-out test_set)
delong_result <- roc.test(roc_logit, roc_final, method = "delong")
print(delong_result)

cat(sprintf(
  "\nRandom Forest AUC (%.4f) vs. Logistic Regression AUC (%.4f): DeLong z = %.3f, p = %.2e\n",
  auc(roc_final), auc(roc_logit), delong_result$statistic, delong_result$p.value
))
```
